headline_insight: Women make up 72% of the 2,104 respondents (1,518 female vs 586 male), but the product mix behind that majority is almost entirely a country story: the Enhanced Credit Life and Crop Insurance samples match Ghana and Vietnam respondent counts exactly, meaning apparent "gendered product preferences" cannot be separated from where the survey was fielded.
paragraphs: The 2026 Insurance Survey drew 2,104 valid respondents, of whom 1,518 (72%) are women and 586 (28%) are men — a female-majority sample consistent with VisionFund's client base and sufficient, at the aggregate level, to support robust gender-disaggregated analysis. Overall satisfaction sits at a Net Promoter Score of 16.8, built from 43.9% promoters, 28.9% passives and 27.1% detractors. That is a positive but unemphatic result: more than a quarter of insured clients are actively dissatisfied, and the promoter margin over detractors is under 17 points. No external or prior-year benchmark for NPS was supplied in this evidence pack, so we deliberately refrain from characterising 16.8 as strong or weak relative to sector norms — that comparison should be added once a defensible benchmark is available.

On product, health insurance dominates for both genders but far more so for men: 90.8% of male respondents hold health cover against 75.1% of female respondents, a 15.7 percentage-point gap. Women are correspondingly over-represented in Enhanced Credit Life (16.6% vs 5.6%, +11.0pt) and Crop Insurance (8.3% vs 3.6%, +4.7pt). The tempting reading is that women diversify beyond health cover more than men do. We flag caution: the Enhanced Credit Life counts (252 female / 33 male) are identical to Ghana's respondent counts, and the Crop Insurance counts (126 female / 21 male) are identical to Vietnam's. Product type in this dataset is therefore effectively a proxy for country of fielding, and any gender difference in product mix is confounded with the differing gender composition of those national samples. This is a structural feature of the survey design rather than a finding about client preference, and it should be stated as such in any onward use of these figures.

The country distribution itself shows meaningful variation in gender balance. Ghana is the most female-skewed sample (16.6% of all women, 5.6% of all men; +11.0pt), followed by Vietnam (+4.7pt), Zambia (+2.8pt) and Malawi (+1.6pt). Uganda runs the other way, accounting for 19.6% of male respondents but only 10.5% of female respondents (-9.1pt), with Rwanda (-5.1pt), Tanzania (-3.8pt) and Kenya (-2.2pt) also male-tilted. These skews matter for interpretation: any indicator that varies by country will appear to vary by gender in the pooled data, and we recommend that all subsequent sections in this report present country-controlled comparisons where sample sizes permit. The Latin America respondents — Bolivia, Ecuador, Honduras (n=1 each), Mexico (n=5) and the Dominican Republic (n=1) — are far too small to support any inference and are reported here only for completeness of the sampling frame; they should be treated as illustrative of coverage, not as evidence of anything.

Finally, a note on evidence balance. This section's pack contains no verbatim client quotations and no divergence flags between quantitative and qualitative findings, so the demographic and NPS picture presented above rests on survey counts alone. Client voice is drawn on in the substantive sections that follow. For programming, the immediate implications are twofold. First, VisionFund's insurance portfolio reaches women at scale, but the depth of that reach is uneven — the 15.7-point health-cover gap warrants investigation as to whether it reflects genuine access barriers for women or simply the country composition described above. Second, the qualitative research design for the next survey round should deliberately over-sample men in Ghana and Vietnam and women in Uganda, so that product and gender can be disentangled rather than inferred. As general sector context — not a finding from this survey — women's lower uptake of formal health cover is a widely discussed pattern in financial inclusion literature; confirming or refuting it for VisionFund's clients requires a design that does not conflate product line with geography.
